a row means. Do NOT copy it back here; issue 1095 is what that cost.

c:accepted_callback_t.why: the callback is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041), so its type belongs to the action server/client rather than to the executor's add call. rclc's counterparts are passed to `rclc_executor_add_action_server` / `_client` -- the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule, seen as a type. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_callback_t`. RESOLVED (issue 0796): our three languages agree again. C takes this third callback at `nros_action_server_init`, Rust takes it at `DeclaredNode::create_action_server_with_callbacks(goal, cancel, accepted)`, and `nros::ActionServer<A>` now has `set_accepted_callback` / `set_accepted_callback_with_ctx` -- matching its existing per-callback setter shape rather than C's all-at-once init. Until then a C++ user who returned ACCEPT_AND_DEFER was never told the goal had been accepted, which is the point at which a deferred goal is supposed to start executing. The hook fires after the accept reply has reached the client, for ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE and ACCEPT_AND_DEFER alike. Phase 379 W3.

c:action_*wait_set*.why: rcl's wait-set protocol -- the caller asks each entity how many wait-set slots it needs and then reads back which of them are ready. RFC-0002's executor drives entities directly through the RMW vtable, so there is no wait set. See the pubsub and service stages' identical rows.

c:action_accept_new_goal.why: rcl allocates a goal handle and returns it; ours accepts by RETURN VALUE from the goal callback (`NROS_GOAL_ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE` / `_AND_DEFER`) or, on the L1 tier, by `nros_action_server_accept_goal_raw(server, goal_id, sequence_number)`. our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`.

c:action_cancel_goal.why: OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE ON SHAPE, no longer on presence: rclcpp_action returns a future from `Client::async_cancel_goal`; ours sends the CancelGoal request and reports the outcome through the client's cancel channel (RFC-0021, no futures) -- Rust's `ActionClient::cancel_goal` returns a `Promise` the caller drives with the executor. That part is a divergence with a reason. The part that was NOT: C++ had no client-side cancel in its callback tier at all. Fixed by issue 0796 -- `nros::ActionClient<A>` now has `cancel_goal(goal_id)` plus `try_recv_cancel_response(CancelReturnCode&)`, the same fire-then-read shape as this C entry point, so all three languages can cancel a goal they started. `nros::PollingActionClient<A>::send_cancel_request` remains the L1 tier's spelling. Phase 379 W3.

c:action_cancel_request_t.why: rcl's `action_msgs/srv/CancelGoal` request struct. Ours never surfaces the request as a type: `nros_action_server_try_recv_cancel_request_raw` writes the named goal id, the service sequence number and the goal's current status into caller storage. and the payload is CDR bytes (`const uint8_t*, size_t`) rather than rcl's `void* ros_message`, because the C ABI has no runtime typesupport -- the only publish in the whole C surface is `nros_publish_raw`. See the pubsub stage's `c:publish_raw` and `c:message_type_t`.

c:action_cancel_response_*.why: rcl builds the `action_msgs/srv/CancelGoal` response as a heap array of `goal_info` sized by `rcl_action_process_cancel_request`, so it needs an init/fini pair and an allocator. Ours is `nros_action_server_send_cancel_reply_raw(server, sequence_number, return_code, accepted[16][], count)`: the caller names the goals it accepted out of its own storage and the arena writes the reply. No allocator, so the response cannot be a constructed object. Our `nros_cancel_response_t` is a different thing -- the per-goal ACCEPT/REJECT decision; see `c:cancel_return_code_t`.

c:action_client_*_callback_t.why: the callback is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041), so its type belongs to the action server/client rather than to the executor's add call. rclc's counterparts are passed to `rclc_executor_add_action_server` / `_client` -- the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule, seen as a type. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_callback_t`.

c:action_client_action_server_is_ready.why:
RE-VERDICTED extension -> their-rename 2026-09-05 (phase-425). `extension` means "ROS 2 has none"; rcl has `rcl_action_server_is_available` and rclcpp_action has `Client::action_server_is_ready`, so the capability is not ours-only and only the C spelling is. The row's SECOND finding is untouched and is not this verdict's: we ship the probe in C and Rust and NOT in C++, which is a real gap in `nros::ActionClient<A>` / `nros::PollingActionClient<A>`. Pair: `c:action_server_is_available`. No code change.

ORIGINAL ROW: OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: the non-blocking server-visibility probe. rcl's is the misnamed `rcl_action_server_is_available`; rclcpp_action's is `Client::action_server_is_ready`. We have it in C and in Rust (`ActionClient::action_server_is_ready`) and NOT in C++ -- neither `nros::ActionClient<A>` nor `nros::PollingActionClient<A>` has a readiness predicate, so a C++ caller can only block in `wait_for_action_server`. Rust also ships it twice: `ActionClient::action_server_is_ready` beside `ActionClientCore::is_server_ready`, exactly the three-spelling mess the service stage recorded at `rust:ClientTrait::is_server_ready`. See `c:action_server_is_available` for the rcl naming half. Phase 379 W3/W5.

majority: the READY word for a client-side readiness probe is rclcpp's and rclrs's elsewhere too -- both recorded surfaces carry `service_is_ready`
their_rename.outlier: `rcl_action_server_is_available` -- rcl alone says AVAILABLE, and names a CLIENT-side probe after the server; the recorded rclc surface has `is_available` only in rcl's two readiness functions

c:action_client_get_action_name.why: OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: reads back the action a client or server was created on. Our C has neither `nros_action_client_get_action_name` nor the server form; our C++ has `get_action_name` on the POLLING tiers ONLY -- and `nros::ActionServer<A>` carries a `char action_name_[256]` field plus a comment saying it exists 'for `get_action_name()` accessor' that was never written; our Rust has `nros_core::ActionServer::name`, which `nros` does not re-export. Four surfaces, one accessor. Same class as the service stage's `cpp:Client::get_service_name` and the pubsub stage's `rust:Publisher::topic_name`. Phase 379 W3.

c:action_client_get_options.why: reads back the options an action client was created with. `nros_action_client_options_t` ships, and so does `nros_action_client_get_default_options`; what is missing is the READBACK -- no `*_get_options` exists anywhere in our C surface, for any entity. See the service stage's `c:client_get_options`. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said there is no runtime options struct. Seven ship and the correlator buckets all fourteen items `same` -- `nros_{node,publisher,subscription,service,client,action_client,action_server}_options_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:1461,1729,2011,2474,2537,2556,2592`) plus a `*_get_default_options` for each, and `nros_node_options_t::domain_id_override` is a RUNTIME per-node domain. What is genuinely absent is the LIFECYCLE around one: no `*_options_copy`, no `*_options_fini`, and no `*_get_options` readback anywhere in the C surface.

c:action_client_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our method-style naming; see the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized`.

c:action_client_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl; our handles carry their state inline because there is no allocator to put it behind a pointer. See the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_impl_t`.

c:action_client_init_default.why: rclc's default-QoS wrapper; `nros_action_client_init` takes no QoS and IS the default form. See the service stage's `c:client_init_default`.

c:action_client_init_polling.why: RFC-0022's polling tier for actions: an entity a task drains itself instead of receiving a callback, for code that owns its own loop. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:action_client_init_with_options.why: our own options-taking entry point, carrying what a device varies per action client (scheduling context) where rcl would use `rcl_action_client_options_t`. See the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_init_with_options`.

c:action_client_is_valid.why:
CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417 W-M2): verdicted `extension`, which means "we add it and ROS 2 has none". The row is THEIRS-ONLY -- `rcl_action_client_is_valid` is rcl's, and the row's own text describes it as "rcl's validity predicate" -- so the verdict asserted the opposite of the bucket. It is a `divergence`: rcl asks a BOOLEAN, we answer with a three-state lifecycle on the handle, which is a reshaped answer to the same question rather than a capability we invented.

rcl's validity predicate. Ours is `nros_action_client_state_t` on the handle -- a three-state lifecycle (uninitialised / callback-mode / polling-mode) rather than a boolean, so double-init and use-after-fini return a code instead of being undefined. See the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_state_t`. Recorded as the theirs half; ours is `c:action_client_state_t`.

c:action_client_poll.why: drains the client's four reply channels once and dispatches the bound callbacks, without the executor. rclcpp_action has no counterpart because its executor always owns dispatch. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:action_client_send_*_raw.why: RFC-0022's polling tier for actions: an entity a task drains itself instead of receiving a callback, for code that owns its own loop. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:action_client_set_*.why: rcl lets a caller install a notify-on-arrival hook per action channel AFTER creation, so a wait set can attach itself to an existing entity. Ours is bound at creation and the notify half is the `_wake_callback` family, which fires the platform's own wake primitive rather than a wait set we do not have. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_set_on_new_message_callback`.

c:action_client_set_*_wake_callback.why: the platform wake primitive fired when a reply or feedback lands on one of the client's four channels, so a task blocked on the platform's own primitive is released without the executor polling. rcl's nearest is the `set_*_client_callback` family, which notifies a wait set we do not have. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_set_wake_callback`.

c:action_client_set_feedback_callback.why: the ours-only setter for `c:feedback_callback_t`. rcl's nearest is `rcl_action_client_set_feedback_subscription_callback`, which notifies a wait set; see `c:action_client_set_*`.

c:action_client_state_t.why: explicit entity lifecycle so double-init and use-after-fini return a code instead of being undefined, and so the L1 and L2 tiers are distinguishable at runtime. See the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_state_t`.

c:action_client_try_recv_*_raw.why: RFC-0022's polling tier for actions: an entity a task drains itself instead of receiving a callback, for code that owns its own loop. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:action_client_wait_for_action_server.why: blocks until the action's send_goal queryable is discoverable, driving the executor. RFC-0021: a blocking helper takes the executor and drives it, which is what makes the timeout reliable on a single-threaded transport. rclcpp_action's `Client::wait_for_action_server` folds onto ours by the *Base rule; rclc has no counterpart. See the service stage's `c:client_wait_for_service`.

c:action_execute.why: rclcpp_action's `ServerGoalHandle::execute()`, moved off the handle onto `(server, goal)`. our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`.

c:action_expire_goals.why: rcl reclaims a completed goal's result after `result_timeout` (15 min by default) and reports which goals expired. Issue 0796 gave us the RECLAMATION half -- `ActionServerCore` compacts the result slab and evicts completed results (delivered-first, then oldest) whenever a completion needs room, plus an eager `expire_completed_results()` -- so the slab no longer only grows and the overflow is no longer silent (`complete_goal_raw` returns `Result`). What is still theirs-only is the C ENTRY POINT and the TIMEOUT: there is no `nros_action_expire_goals`, and the trigger is memory pressure rather than a clock, because the core is `no_std` with no time source threaded through it. A caller cannot ask 'which goals expired' and cannot set a per-goal `result_timeout`. Phase 379 W3.

c:action_get_*names_and_types*.why: no dynamic discovery: peers are static (RFC-0036), so there is no graph to enumerate action names and types out of. See the graph stage.

c:action_get_goal_status.why: the authoritative per-goal status query, answered from the arena rather than from a field on the handle -- `NROS_RET_NOT_FOUND` once the arena has retired the goal. rcl's counterpart is `rcl_action_goal_handle_get_status` on the handle object; our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`.

c:action_get_goal_status_array.why: the read half of `c:action_publish_status`. The per-goal query ours offers is `nros_action_get_goal_status(server, goal, status*)` and the sweep is C++'s `ActionServer::for_each_active_goal`; neither materialises an array, because there is no allocator to materialise it into. A user loses the ability to read every goal's status as one message.

c:action_get_result.why: the blocking get_result: send the request and drive the executor until the result or the timeout. See `c:action_send_goal`.

c:action_get_zero_initialized_*.why: rcl's free-function zero-init spelling; ours is the method-style `nros_action_client_get_zero_initialized` / `nros_action_server_get_zero_initialized`. See the pubsub stage's `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`. The goal-handle, goal-info, cancel-request/response and status-array forms have no counterpart at all because we ship none of those types; see `c:action_goal_handle_*` and `c:action_cancel_response_*`.

c:action_goal_event_e.why: the event alphabet of `c:action_transition_goal_state`; we name transitions with verbs instead. See that row.

c:action_goal_handle_*.why: our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`.

c:action_goal_info_t.why: rcl's goal id + acceptance timestamp. Ours carries the id alone (`nros_goal_uuid_t`) at the C boundary: the stamp is filled by the arena when it publishes status, and an image with no clock source (RFC-0036: time is a board capability) cannot be asked to supply one at accept time. `nros_core::GoalInfo` keeps both fields for the wire.

c:action_goal_state_t.why:
RE-VERDICTED declined -> their-rename 2026-09-05 (phase-425). The W5 re-verdict got the ARGUMENT right and had no verdict to put it under. `declined` reads "ROS 2 has it, we deliberately do not", and we DO have it -- `nros_goal_status_t`, in all three languages. What we decline is rcl's WORD, which is a different sentence and is what `their-rename` is for. The evidence the W5 text assembled is unchanged and is now in `their_rename`. Pair: `c:goal_status_t`. No code change; no target name invented.

ORIGINAL ROW: RE-VERDICTED rename -> declined 2026-08-27 (phase-379 W5). The row's own evidence settles it: rcl is the odd speller. `action_msgs/msg/GoalStatus` is the wire type, and rclcpp_action, our C (`nros_goal_status_t`), our C++ (`nros::GoalStatus`) and our Rust (`GoalStatus`) all say STATUS; `rcl_action_goal_state_t` says STATE alone. `rename` means OURS is the one that should change, which is false here, so the verdict was wrong even though the prose was right. Declined: rcl has this spelling, we deliberately do not, and the reason is that ours follows the message. No code change; no target name invented. ORIGINAL ROW (verdict was `rename`): rcl's name for what we call `nros_goal_status_t`, and both mirror `action_msgs/msg/GoalStatus`. rclcpp_action and our C++ and Rust all say STATUS (`GoalStatus`), rcl alone says STATE; ours agrees with the majority and with the message. Recorded as a rename so the pair is visible, but this is one where THEIRS is the odd spelling -- see `c:goal_status_t` for our half.

rename.resolution: Not a rename. Theirs-only, and theirs is the outlier — ours already agrees with rclcpp_action and with `action_msgs/msg/GoalStatus`. Re-verdicted to `declined`. SUPERSEDED 2026-09-05 (phase-425): `declined` was the nearest of the five verdicts that existed, and it was still false of the capability. The row is now `their-rename`, the verdict written for exactly this sentence; see `why`.

majority: `action_msgs/msg/GoalStatus` -- the wire type both sides serialize
their_rename.outlier: `rcl_action_goal_state_t` -- rcl alone calls the enum a STATE, while the message it mirrors and the status types beside it in the same header say STATUS

c:action_goal_status_array_*.why: rcl hands the caller a heap `GoalStatusArray` to fill and publish (`rcl_action_get_goal_status_array` + `rcl_action_publish_status`). Ours is not a user-facing object at all: the arena keeps the status of every live goal and publishes the array itself on every transition (`ActionServerCore::publish_status_array`). No allocator to build the array with, and nothing for a caller to do with it. See `c:action_publish_status`.

c:action_goal_status_t.why: rcl's `action_msgs/msg/GoalStatus` C struct (goal_info + status byte). Ours splits the two: `nros_goal_status_t` is the status ENUM and the stamped pair exists only inside the arena (`nros_core::GoalStatusStamped`), because a C caller never receives one -- the arena publishes the status topic itself. See `c:action_publish_status`.

c:action_notify_goal_done.why: rcl makes the caller tell the server a goal reached a terminal state, because the goal handle and the server are separate objects that must be kept in step. Ours cannot drift: `nros_action_succeed` / `_abort` / `_canceled` retire the goal in the arena as part of the same call. A user loses nothing; there is no second place for the fact to live.

c:action_process_cancel_request.why: rcl matches a `CancelGoal` request against its goal handles and builds the response array for the caller. Ours splits the same work: the arena matches, the user's `nros_cancel_callback_t` decides per goal, and `nros_action_server_send_cancel_reply_raw` writes the reply on the L1 tier. The matching cannot be a caller-visible step because the goal set lives in the arena, not in caller storage. our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`.

c:action_publish_feedback.why: one of the eight the first report could not explain, and it decomposes into two changes that both have a reason. (1) The payload is `(const uint8_t*, size_t)` where rcl takes `void* ros_feedback`: and the payload is CDR bytes (`const uint8_t*, size_t`) rather than rcl's `void* ros_message`, because the C ABI has no runtime typesupport -- the only publish in the whole C surface is `nros_publish_raw`. See the pubsub stage's `c:publish_raw` and `c:message_type_t`. (2) The goal is a SEPARATE parameter beside the server, where rcl takes the server alone and rclc takes the goal handle alone. rcl can, because its `void* ros_feedback` is the whole `<Action>_FeedbackMessage` envelope and the goal_id is a FIELD inside it; rclc can, because `rclc_action_goal_handle_t` carries a pointer back to its server. Ours can do neither: RFC-0069 makes the core write the envelope (one CDR header, then the goal id, then the fields) so the caller supplies only the inner feedback and the id must arrive as an argument, and our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `nros_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `nros_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`. Both halves follow from decisions taken elsewhere, so this is a divergence rather than an unexplained signature -- but it is the widest signature in the action API and it is worth saying that the L1 sibling `nros_action_server_publish_feedback_raw` spells the same call `(server, goal_id[16], feedback_cdr, len)`, i.e. the same four values with a different goal spelling.

c:action_publish_status.why: the `<action>/status` topic is published by the arena on every goal transition (`ActionServerCore::publish_status_array`), not by the user. Exposing the verb would let an image publish a status array that disagrees with the arena, which is the state the arena exists to be the only copy of. A user loses the ability to publish status on their own cadence.

c:action_send_*.why: rcl_action exposes the action's three services and two topics one message at a time so a caller can drive the protocol itself. Ours runs the protocol inside the executor's action arena and hands the user the DECISIONS (accept/reject, cancel accept/reject) and the payloads; the part a caller may drive is the L1 polling tier (`nros_action_server_try_recv_goal_request_raw`, `nros_action_client_send_goal_raw`, ...), which is RFC-0022's polling tier for actions -- see the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`. and the payload is CDR bytes (`const uint8_t*, size_t`) rather than rcl's `void* ros_message`, because the C ABI has no runtime typesupport -- the only publish in the whole C surface is `nros_publish_raw`. See the pubsub stage's `c:publish_raw` and `c:message_type_t`.

c:action_send_goal.why: the blocking convenience: send the goal and drive the executor until the server accepts or rejects. rclcpp_action's equivalent is `async_send_goal(...).get()`, which deadlocks on a single-threaded executor -- the reason RFC-0021 makes the executor an explicit parameter. See the service stage's `cpp:Client::call`.

c:action_send_goal_async.why: rclcpp_action returns a `std::shared_future<GoalHandle::SharedPtr>`; ours writes the generated goal uuid into caller storage and delivers the accept/reject to `nros_goal_response_callback_t`. No futures and no async runtime (RFC-0021); no allocator for the shared goal handle. See the service stage's `cpp:Client::async_send_request`.

c:action_server_*_raw.why: RFC-0022's polling tier for actions: an entity a task drains itself instead of receiving a callback, for code that owns its own loop. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:action_server_active_goal_count_raw.why:
DEPRECATED ALIAS, phase-379 W6 decision 3 (2026-09-03). The live spelling is `nros_action_server_get_active_goal_count(server, size_t *out) -> nros_ret_t`, which carries the substantive verdict and the full account of the merge. This name survives in the public surface as an `NROS_DEPRECATED_MSG` `static inline` forwarder in `nros/action.h`, so an out-of-tree C node that still names it keeps compiling and gets a diagnostic naming its replacement. Recorded rather than left implicit for the same reason as `c:param_declare_*` in param.json and `rust:BoardConfig::zenoh_locator` in boot.json: a deprecated item is still API a reader can find.

THE FORWARDER PRESERVES THE OLD `int32_t` TRI-STATE, which is the fiddly part, because the function it delegates to is wider in two directions at once. Old contract: `>= 0` is the count, `NROS_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT` for NULL or not-a-polling-server, `NROS_RET_NOT_INIT` when built without `rmw-cffi`. Three things the forwarder does to hold that:
1. It re-applies the TIER GATE itself (`server == NULL || server->state != NROS_ACTION_SERVER_STATE_POLLING` -> NROS_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT) before delegating. The merged function deliberately answers a callback-tier server too; this name promised the polling tier only, so without the gate a `_raw` caller holding an INITIALIZED server would start getting a COUNT where it used to get an error. The struct is public and `state` is a public field, so a header-only forwarder can do this.
2. It narrows `size_t` back to `int32_t` explicitly, returning `NROS_RET_ERROR` above INT32_MAX. The old body's bare `as i32` would have wrapped a large count into a negative value a caller reads as an error code. Unreachable in practice -- both the arena and the inline core hold a fixed-capacity goal array orders of magnitude below INT32_MAX -- but the conversion is now stated rather than inherited.
3. It passes the merged function's `nros_ret_t` straight through on failure, so NOT_INIT stays NOT_INIT.

ONE DOCUMENTED DIFFERENCE, in a build WITHOUT `rmw-cffi` only: the old function returned `NROS_RET_NOT_INIT` for any non-NULL server regardless of state, where the forwarder returns `NROS_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT` for a non-POLLING one. The old behaviour disagreed with ITSELF across the feature flag (the `rmw-cffi` build returned INVALID_ARGUMENT there); the forwarder keeps the meaningful half. For a POLLING server in that build both old and new answer NOT_INIT.

rust:RequestedGoal.why: rclrs 0.7.0 models a goal's life as a TYPESTATE chain -- `RequestedGoal` -> `AcceptedGoal` -> `ExecutingGoal` -> `TerminatedGoal`, each a distinct type whose methods are only the transitions legal from that state, with the goal moved from one to the next. Ours keeps goals in a STATIC ARENA addressed by UUID (`nros_goal_uuid_t` / `GoalId`), and the server asks the arena about a goal rather than holding it. The constraint is that a typestate chain hands the application an owning handle per goal, and with no allocator and a fixed-capacity arena the storage cannot follow the handle -- MAX_GOALS is declared at build time and the arena outlives every borrow of it. RFC-0069. Note ROS 2 does not agree with ITSELF here: rclcpp_action uses `async_send_goal` and shared `ClientGoalHandle`, rclrs 0.7.0 uses `request_goal` and the typestate chain, so 'match ROS 2' has no single answer for actions -- W5 has to pick a side and say which.

rust:RosAction.why: the trait a generated action type implements: the three user types, the five wire envelopes, the action and per-service RIHS hashes, and `register_protocol_types`. rclrs 0.5.1 ships NO action API at all -- the recorded surface has zero action, goal or feedback items -- so every action item in our Rust API is ours-only by construction rather than by an RTOS need. The convergence point is whenever rclrs grows actions; until then there is nothing to be a divergence FROM. The envelope split is RFC-0069's -- the generated code owns the wire shape so the core writes exactly one CDR header. Compare the service stage's `rust:RosService`.

cpp:Server::Server<ActionT>.why: phase-417 stage 0 — visible only because `rclcpp_compat.hpp` is now a translation unit (issue 1020). The shim ships this TYPE as a name, so its members stop inheriting "we do not have this type" and become their own claim. Not a new gap: a gap INSIDE a type we ship is a different statement from one about a type we do not. `rclcpp_action::Server`'s member surface is the wait-set/`Waitable` protocol (`execute`, `is_ready`, `set_on_ready_callback`) plus `make_shared`; the executor owns readiness here and entities are arena-registered at creation (RFC-0002), so there is nothing for a caller to poll or construct.
